methodological_rigor.justification: This is a single-center retrospective cohort study of synchronous bone-metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate cancer patients diagnosed from 2017–2023, with explicit inclusion/exclusion criteria and a final cohort of 203 patients (after excluding 28 lost to follow-up). The design is appropriate for identifying prognostic factors and treatment-timing associations, and the authors explicitly use 3- and 6-month landmark analyses to mitigate immortal time bias in evaluating early initiation of novel hormonal agents. Cox regression and Kaplan–Meier analyses are standard for OS, but residual confounding and treatment-selection bias remain likely in an observational real-world setting, and the Discussion acknowledges unstable estimates in some subgroups and missing prognostic covariates (e.g., continuous PSA modeling limitations).

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: This is an individual retrospective cohort assessing survival associations with disease features and treatment timing, consistent with Oxford LoE 2b. Clinical relevance is high because the cohort is high-risk (e.g., 83.7% high-volume disease) and overall survival is the primary endpoint, with landmark analyses showing early novel hormonal agent initiation within 3 months is associated with lower mortality risk (HR 0.55, P<0.001). While causality cannot be inferred, the findings support earlier intensification strategies in routine management of de novo bone-metastatic HSPC.

reporting_quality.justification: STROBE is the relevant standard for this retrospective cohort, and the manuscript reports cohort derivation, outcome definition (OS), key covariates (including high-volume disease), and analytic choices including landmark analysis to address immortal time bias. Reporting would be stronger with clearer detail on handling of missingness and fuller presentation of model covariates and diagnostics, especially given acknowledged limitations in PSA recording (>70% categorical for PSA >100 ng/mL). No data/code sharing is described, so external reproducibility is limited.

novelty_literature.justification: The central finding that earlier use of intensified systemic therapy improves outcomes in metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate cancer is consistent with the broader literature, so conceptual novelty is limited. The manuscript’s added value is focusing on the synchronous bone-metastatic subset in a contemporary Chinese tertiary-center cohort and explicitly applying landmark methods to address immortal time bias for early-treatment questions. Overall this is an incremental but useful real-world contribution.

writing_presentation.justification: The manuscript is generally clear in stating aims, defining SBM-HSPC, and summarizing key results (incidence 6.09%, median OS 43 months, HR 0.55 for early NHA). It also provides an unusually detailed limitations discussion (e.g., confounding, single-center generalizability, PSA data granularity) that appropriately tempers causal interpretations. Some Discussion passages speculate on temporal incidence shifts and screening/imaging drivers without direct supporting data in the cohort, which could be framed more cautiously.

key_strengths: Well-defined retrospective cohort with a substantial sample for a single-center metastatic subset (final n=203) and OS-based outcomes.
Uses landmark analyses (3 and 6 months) to reduce immortal time bias when assessing the association between early novel hormonal agent initiation and survival.
Findings are clinically actionable in direction (earlier intensification associated with better OS) and presented with quantitative hazard ratios.
key_concerns: Observational design with likely treatment-selection bias and residual confounding; early initiation may be a proxy for performance status, access, or other unmeasured factors.
Some key covariates are limited or coarse (e.g., PSA recorded categorically for many high values), and subgroup estimates are described as unstable.
Single-center setting limits generalizability and the study does not provide external validation or prospective confirmation.
chief_reviewer.rationale: The paper is methodologically thoughtful for a retrospective cohort (notably the landmark analysis) and addresses an important high-risk population, but tier-2 acceptance would likely require stronger confounding control and clearer causal framing.
